title: The Hidden Factor in Student Success: Family Structure | Institute for Family Studies
gist: A truncated excerpt of an Ian Rowe and Brad Wilcox Wall Street Journal op-ed arguing that the annual fight over racial composition at New York's elite exam high schools ignores family structure: 80% of Asian children nationwide live with married birth parents versus 30% of black children, a gap they say predicts academic outcomes as well as or better than race. The record is only the opening section, ending at 'Continues...'.

insights.claim: Only three of the 777 students in Stuyvesant High School's incoming class this year are black, reigniting annual demands that New York City scrap the specialized high school entrance exam.
insights.speaker: Ian Rowe, Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: A concrete number that sets the political stakes on exam-based admissions--policy risk for education-selection regimes and for NYC school governance.
insights.quote: Only three of the 777 students in Stuyvesant High School’s incoming class this year are black.

insights.claim: Queens Borough President Donovan Richards has characterized the outcome as black students 'being locked out' and as segregation, showing that elected officials are framing test-based admission as a civil-rights violation rather than a measurement question.
insights.speaker: Ian Rowe, Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Elected-official framing predicts the direction of policy; testing-based selection faces removal risk in large districts.

themes.theme: Family structure as the omitted variable

insights.claim: Census Bureau American Community Survey data show 80% of Asian children nationwide live with married birth parents versus 30% of black children, a 50-point gap the authors say is systematically absent from debates about race in American schools.
insights.speaker: Ian Rowe, Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: A hard, publicly sourced number that reframes achievement-gap analysis around household composition rather than school inputs.
insights.quote: 80% of Asian children nationwide live with married birth parents, vs. 30% of black children

insights.claim: Whether a child has two married parents at home predicts school success--and admission to a school like Stuyvesant--almost as well as or even better than race does.
insights.speaker: Ian Rowe, Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: If household structure dominates race as a predictor, interventions aimed at test design will not move outcomes; the actionable variable sits upstream of schooling.
insights.quote: This factor—whether a child has two married parents at home—predicts success in school, or admission to a school like Stuyvesant, almost as well as or even better than race.

insights.claim: The authors' central contrarian claim is that family structure is entirely missing from the public debate over racial disparities at elite public high schools, making it an omitted-variable problem rather than a data-availability problem.
insights.speaker: Ian Rowe, Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Identifies a blind spot in mainstream education-policy discourse--where a contrarian analytical edge exists on the achievement-gap question.
insights.quote: Missing from the debate is any discussion of family structure.
